title: Why does Spring recommend putting @Transactional on the concrete implementation class rather than on the interface?
keyPoints: Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB proxies (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true) which create a subclass of the concrete class
CGLIB proxies read annotations from the target class, so @Transactional on the interface may be silently ignored
JDK dynamic proxies implement the interface and can read annotations placed there
Placing @Transactional on the implementation class works for both proxy types, making it the portable choice
AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource scans the target class first, so implementation annotations always win
Self-invocation (this.method()) bypasses the proxy entirely, so no transaction is started regardless of annotation placement

s1_definition.oneliner: Spring Boot uses CGLIB proxies by default which read annotations from the concrete class, so placing @Transactional on the implementation is the only placement that works reliably for both CGLIB and JDK proxy types.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **CGLIB proxy** -- the Spring Boot default (`spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true`), creates a runtime subclass of the concrete class and reads `@Transactional` from the class hierarchy.
- **JDK dynamic proxy** -- an interface-based proxy that implements the bean's interface and can read `@Transactional` from interface methods.
- **AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource** -- the component that scans for `@Transactional`; it checks the target class first, so implementation annotations always take precedence.
- **Self-invocation pitfall** -- calling `this.method()` bypasses the proxy entirely, so no transaction is started regardless of where the annotation is placed.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, there is a job description (interface) and the actual employee (implementation). A visitor (proxy) asks the employee directly for a signature. If the signature policy is written only on the job description but the visitor looks at the employee's badge, the policy is missed. Placing the policy on the employee's badge (implementation) ensures it is always seen, regardless of whether the visitor checks the job description or the badge.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  JDK Dynamic Proxy:
  ┌─────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ TransferService     │     │ TransferServiceImpl   │
  │ (interface)         │     │ (concrete class)      │
  │ @Transactional ✓    │◀────│                       │
  └─────────────────────┘     └──────────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
  JDK Proxy implements interface
  -> reads @Transactional from interface ✓

  CGLIB Proxy (Spring Boot default):
  ┌─────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ TransferService     │     │ TransferServiceImpl   │
  │ (interface)         │     │ (concrete class)      │
  │ @Transactional ?    │     │ @Transactional ✓      │
  └─────────────────────┘     └──────────┬───────────┘
                                         │
                                         ▼
                              CGLIB Proxy extends class
                              -> reads @Transactional from class ✓
                              -> may MISS interface annotation ✗

  Safe placement: always on implementation
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Spring Boot uses CGLIB proxies by default, and CGLIB proxies create a subclass of the concrete class. They read @Transactional from the class hierarchy, not necessarily from the interface. Placing the annotation only on the interface means the CGLIB proxy may silently skip it, and the method runs without a transaction. Placing it on the implementation works for both CGLIB and JDK proxies, which is why Spring's documentation recommends it.

In the National Bank of India transfer service, Rajesh initially placed @Transactional on the TransferService interface. The application ran fine in development, but under Spring Boot's default CGLIB proxy the annotation was silently ignored. Transfers ran without a transaction boundary, and a partial failure left accounts inconsistent. Moving the annotation to TransferServiceImpl fixed the problem immediately.

A senior engineer also watches for two silent killers: self-invocation (calling this.method() bypasses the proxy entirely) and @Transactional on private or final methods (CGLIB cannot subclass them). Both fail silently with no compile-time or runtime error. Use SonarQube or ArchUnit to catch these at build time.

Remember one sentence: always put @Transactional on the implementation class, because CGLIB proxies read from the class, not the interface.
